decisions.reason: City counters, census commute data and trip surveys can show how often Edmonton’s bike lanes are used and why counts, riders and trip shares are different measures.
Census and transportation survey data can show cyclists’ occupations, incomes, education and vehicle ownership rather than relying on anecdotes about who rides.
Monthly counter totals and weather records can show how many people ride through winter, under what conditions and whether winter cycling has grown.
The snow policy, service schedules and council reports can show when bike lanes and streets are cleared, where snow is placed and what changes are proposed.

Before-and-after traffic counts and travel times on converted corridors can show whether reallocating lanes changed congestion, while the general claim about roads carrying services adds nothing checkable.
Design drawings, lane-width standards and pavement-condition records can show what space remains for vehicles and whether the street developed the problems residents describe.
Capital budgets and project cost sheets can put the active-transportation allocation beside road spending and test each percentage and project comparison on the same basis.
The $100 million approval is common ground throughout this source, so checking the council vote would only restate an undisputed budget fact.
Infrastructure-condition reports and budgets can show the size of Edmonton’s renewal shortfall, what was funded and whether money was actually redirected from the cited services.
City tax-rate and typical-property records can show the general increase, although the two anonymous residents’ dollar amounts cannot be verified without their assessment and tax notices.
Administration’s report and recorded votes can show what pause was recommended, which motions were made and how each councillor voted, without examining the allegation about councillors’ motives.
The hearing record can establish the speaker balance and time limit, but the claim that supporters were paid or organized should be dropped unless the lobbyist registry links them directly.
Contracts, purchase records and the tender calendar can show which routes were already committed and whether they could still have been tendered for 2026.
Project engagement records can show whom the City consulted and what participants said, while the claim about most Edmontonians should be dropped unless a representative citywide survey exists.
Election results, candidates’ published positions and provincial recall law can show turnout and recall rules, though they cannot establish what every voter knew when voting.
The remuneration rules can settle the vehicle-allowance claim, while the blanket claim that councillors never bike should be dropped unless their own disclosures provide a complete answer.
Salary disclosures and filed interest statements can show the relevant pay and declared interests, without treating either as proof of an improper motive.
Municipal budgets and intergovernmental funding records can show how much road money comes from property taxes, fuel-tax transfers and other sources shared by drivers and cyclists.
Project parking inventories and parking-program accounts can show how many spaces each lane removed and what providing those spaces costs the City.
The zoning bylaw and infill permit records answer questions about parking minimums, tree removal, and density. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Council-approved plans and agreements can show whether Edmonton committed to 15-minute planning or a year-round downtown car ban and what those commitments actually require.
Response-time records and emergency access design standards show whether bike lanes delay or assist emergency vehicles. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Route drawings and accessibility standards can show where barriers, loading areas, driveways and alleys preserve access and where a design creates the cited detour or obstacle.
Published schedules, trip planners, service histories, ridership and collision records can compare transit with driving and test the specific claims about LRT and removed routes.
City collision records and the traffic bylaw answer whether bike lanes improve safety and who is at fault in collisions. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Road-classification maps, route inventories, design files and professional sign-offs can show which street types receive bike lanes and how their designs were approved.
The City’s network map can show where routes connect, where they terminate and whether gaps remain along the LRT.
Project records and the street-level complaint log can establish the lane’s location, installation date and whether complaints were recorded after it opened.
Design drawings and school-location records can show exactly what is being built on each side of 132 Avenue and how many schools sit along the affected stretch.
Written provincial directives and tabled legislation can show whether Edmonton was ordered to stop building bike lanes and whether legislation was actually proposed.
The design file, approval history and correspondence can show what was proposed outside the school, the councillor’s official role and why the design stopped.
The project record can show when the 189 Street lane was installed and removed, which official decisions authorized it and what removal cost.
Municipal project and council records can identify Canadian cities that have removed bike lanes and distinguish isolated removals from a broader trend.

Reopen this when business closures can be linked to customer-access changes through location-level records or owner evidence, because closure counts alone cannot establish why businesses failed. The two readers split NO and PARK.
